blocks.text: An MCP server that runs on one machine has one way to fail completely.
High availability means designing the deployment so that no single instance, zone, or region can take the whole system down.
This lesson covers redundancy, multi zone and multi region setups, automatic failover, and the real cost tradeoffs behind all of it.
1. What a Single Point of Failure Really Is

blocks.alt: What a Single Point of Failure Really Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308227-299530976.png
A single point of failure is any one component that, if it stops working, takes the entire system down with it.
One MCP instance, one database, one network link, and one power source are all classic examples.
High availability work is mostly the process of finding these one off components and giving each of them a backup.

blocks.title: Redundancy is not optional extra
blocks.content: If removing one component causes a full outage, that component is a single point of failure, no matter how reliable it seems.

blocks.text: 2. Redundancy at Every Layer
Redundancy has to exist at every layer that could fail, not just the obvious one.
That includes compute instances, load balancers, DNS, databases, and even the network path between zones.

items: Compute, run more than one instance of the MCP server.
Load balancing, use more than one load balancer or a managed one with its own redundancy.
Data, replicate the database or store across multiple nodes.
Network, avoid depending on a single link or a single provider.

blocks.text: Missing redundancy in even one of these layers can undo all the effort spent on the others.
3. Running Across Multiple Availability Zones
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308228-526927765.png
An availability zone is an isolated section of a cloud region, with its own power and networking.
Running MCP instances in at least two or three zones means a single zone outage does not remove the whole service.
Cloud providers design zones to fail independently, so this is one of the cheapest forms of high availability you can buy.
4. Running Across Multiple Regions
A region is a separate geographic area, containing its own set of availability zones.
Multi zone protects against a data center problem. Multi region protects against a whole region going down.
Multi region is more expensive and more complex, since data now has to replicate across much longer distances.

code.content:
# Simplified multi region deployment layout
regions:
  us-east-1:
    zones: [a, b, c]
    instances: 3
    role: primary
  eu-west-1:
    zones: [a, b]
    instances: 2
    role: standby
routing:
  strategy: latency-based
  failover: automatic

blocks.text: This kind of config lets traffic route to the closest healthy region, and fail over automatically if one region goes dark.
5. Health Checks, the Foundation of Failover

blocks.alt: Health Checks, the Foundation of Failover
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308228-141667954.png
None of this works without a reliable way to detect that an instance or zone is actually unhealthy.
A health check is a small, cheap endpoint that reports whether the MCP server can serve real requests right now.
A good health check verifies its own critical dependencies, not just that the process is running.
6. Automatic Failover Configuration
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308229-278594363.png
Failover is the process of automatically shifting traffic away from an unhealthy instance or zone.
This is usually configured on the load balancer or DNS layer, using the health check as the trigger.

code.content:
# Load balancer target group health check
healthCheck:
  path: /health
  intervalSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  healthyThreshold: 2
  unhealthyThreshold: 3
targets:
  - zone: us-east-1a
    instance: mcp-1
  - zone: us-east-1b
    instance: mcp-2
  - zone: us-east-1c
    instance: mcp-3

blocks.text: After three failed checks in a row, that target is pulled out of rotation, no human has to notice or act.
7. How Failover Behaves During a Zone Outage
When a zone fails, its instances start missing health checks within seconds.
The load balancer stops sending traffic there and routes everything to the remaining healthy zones.
Clients never see the failed zone at all, they just experience slightly higher load on the surviving instances.
8. Load Balancing Across Healthy Instances
Once failover removes a bad target, the remaining healthy instances have to absorb its share of traffic.
This only works smoothly if the remaining capacity was already sized to handle one zone being gone.

blocks.title: Size for N minus one
blocks.content: A common rule is to run enough capacity that the system stays healthy even with one full zone removed.

blocks.text: 9. Replicating State and Data
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308229-374272256.png
Stateless MCP instances are easy to fail over, since any instance can take over from any other.
The harder part is usually the data layer, since a database also needs replicas across zones or regions.
Synchronous replication keeps replicas perfectly in sync but adds latency. Asynchronous replication is faster but can lose a few recent writes on failover.
10. DNS and Traffic Routing During Failover
DNS based failover points a domain name at a healthy region when the primary one fails its health checks.
DNS changes take time to propagate, since resolvers cache old answers for a while.
Because of that caching delay, DNS failover is usually a slower, coarser tool than load balancer level failover.
11. Detecting an Outage Before Clients Do
Fast failover depends on fast detection, which means aggressive but not overly sensitive health check intervals.
Checking every few seconds catches failures quickly. Checking too aggressively can cause false alarms during brief load spikes.

items: Interval too long, users notice the outage before the system reacts.
Interval too short, brief slowness can trigger unnecessary failovers.
Multiple consecutive failures, a good middle ground before declaring an instance unhealthy.

blocks.text: 12. Testing Failover on Purpose
A failover path that has never been tested is not something you can trust during a real outage.
Teams intentionally kill an instance or block a zone in a controlled test to confirm traffic actually reroutes.

code.content:
# Simulate a zone outage for a failover test
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0abc123 i-0def456
# watch the load balancer drop these targets
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn>

blocks.text: These game day exercises catch broken failover long before a real outage does.
13. Measuring Availability with Nines
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308229-552575420.png
Availability is usually expressed as a percentage of uptime over a year, often called nines.

blocks.text: Each extra nine costs meaningfully more in infrastructure, testing, and operational discipline.
14. The Cost of High Availability
Every layer of redundancy costs money, running idle standby capacity that mostly sits unused.
Multi region setups also add cross region data transfer costs and extra engineering time to keep in sync.
None of this is free, so the level of high availability chosen should match a real business need, not just best practice instinct.
15. Matching Cost to Downtime Tolerance
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308230-441318111.png
The real question behind any high availability decision is how much downtime the business can actually tolerate.
An internal tool used by a handful of people can often accept an hour of downtime a month without real harm.
A payment critical MCP server used by thousands of paying customers cannot accept the same downtime at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Business context","Reasonable target","Typical setup"],"rows":[["Internal tool, low usage","99 percent to 99.9 percent","Single zone, simple restarts"],["Customer facing, moderate traffic","99.9 percent to 99.95 percent","Multi zone, automatic failover"],["Revenue critical, high traffic","99.99 percent or higher","Multi region, automatic failover, tested regularly"]]}

blocks.text: Spending on multi region infrastructure for a low traffic internal tool is usually wasted money.
Worked Example: Sizing High Availability for an MCP Server
Say an MCP server powers a customer facing product with real revenue impact during downtime.
The team decides on a target of 99.95 percent availability, about 22 minutes of downtime a month.

code.content:
instances:
  region: us-east-1
  zones: [a, b, c]
  countPerZone: 2
healthCheck:
  path: /health
  intervalSeconds: 10
  unhealthyThreshold: 3
database:
  mode: multi-az
  replicas: 2
loadBalancer:
  crossZone: true
  failover: automatic

blocks.text: Six total instances across three zones means losing a whole zone still leaves four instances serving traffic.
The database runs with a synchronous replica in a second zone, so a single zone failure loses no committed data.
Common Mistakes

items: Running every instance in a single availability zone, so one zone outage is a full outage.
Health checks that only confirm the process is alive, missing a broken database connection underneath.
Never testing failover, so the first real test happens during an actual outage.
Buying multi region infrastructure for a system where a short outage barely matters to the business.
Sizing capacity for the happy path, leaving no spare room to absorb traffic when a zone goes down.

blocks.text: Practice
Take an MCP deployment you control and list every component it depends on, one by one.
For each one, ask what happens if it disappears right now, and whether anything else can take over.

code.content:
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn>
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids <one-instance-id>
# confirm traffic keeps flowing through the remaining instances

blocks.text: Then estimate how much downtime your business could actually tolerate, and compare that against what you just found.
Key Takeaway
High availability is redundancy plus automatic detection plus automatic failover, spread across zones or regions.
The right amount of it is not the maximum possible, it is whatever matches how much downtime your business can really afford.
